Friendship and social life

Shyness and social anxiety: when other people are frightening

Being shy is a trait; social anxiety limits your life. We believe others watch us far more than they do.

Speaking in a meeting, making a phone call, walking into a crowded room or eating in front of others. For many people these situations bring nerves. For some, the fear is so intense that they avoid them even when it costs them opportunities.

Shyness and social anxiety

Shyness is a temperament trait: some caution with new people or situations, which usually passes as confidence grows. Social anxiety is more intense: a persistent fear of being judged, humiliated or rejected that leads people to avoid situations or endure them with great distress. An international study estimated that about 4% of people have it at some point in their lives.

The spotlight effect

In 2000, Thomas Gilovich asked students to walk into a room wearing a T-shirt they found embarrassing. They estimated that half the people there would have noticed it; in fact, fewer than a quarter did. This is the spotlight effect: we believe we are under a spotlight that others barely see.

People with social anxiety also often use safety behaviours, such as avoiding eye contact, saying little or rehearsing every sentence. They bring short-term relief but prevent them from finding out the situation was not so dangerous.

Safety behaviours

Many people with social anxiety use strategies to avoid a bad time: avoiding eye contact, mentally rehearsing every sentence, staying in a corner, drinking to loosen up or saying very little so as not to make mistakes. David Clark and Adrian Wells called these safety behaviours. The problem is that they maintain anxiety, because they prevent you from finding out that nothing terrible happens without them, and they also make the person seem more distant. Gradually dropping them is a key part of treatment.

An effective treatment

Cognitive behavioural therapy specific to social anxiety, such as Clark and Wells's model, is the treatment of choice according to clinical guidelines and, in comparative studies, works better than medication in the long term. It includes focusing outwards rather than on oneself, practising feared situations and reviewing video to see how others actually see us.

What usually helps

  • Gradually face feared situations, starting with the easiest.
  • Drop safety behaviours to see what happens without them.
  • Focus on the conversation, not on how you come across.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment with the most evidence for social anxiety.
